Messages.Author: ira...@gmail.com
Messages.Body:
Hello LSJ,

Consider this scenario:

It's midgame, and my only reasonable chance to get a GW is to pass a
vote that my predator can definitely block. Assume the vote will pass
if it reaches referendum. I threaten my predator, "If you block the
vote, I will beat up your vampire and be very vengeful for the rest of
the game."

If the vote passes, my predator will no longer have a reasonable chance
at a game win, but if I beat up his blocking vampire or play
vengefully, he *also* won't have a reasonable chance at a game win. He
chooses to block, presumably hoping that I was bluffing about the
combat or vengefulness.

Once the vote is blocked, I no longer have a reasonable chance at a GW,
but I still have a reasonable chance at more VPs as long as I don't
follow through with my threat. If I beat up my predator's vampire and
play vengefully against him, then I will give up the reasonable chance
at the additional VPs.

Is it legal to follow through with my threat, which was made as my best
attempt towards a game win? If I had to guess, I would say, "No," even
though a lot of people would want to be allowed to be vengeful.

In practice, a player could easily twist definitions of "reasonable" to
justify a wide variety of actions. I'm not asking this question for
judges to enforce a rule. I'm asking this question for the players who
will voluntarily choose to follow the rules once they understand them,
myself included.

Thanks,

Ira

The point is that the threat offers no additional legal support for the
position. If the activity is play-to-win by itself, then it is still
play to win after you'd threated to do it.

If it isn't play-to-win by itself, then having threatened to do it
won't help make it play to win.

Messages.Author: Ben Peal
Messages.Body:
Ira wrote:
> Consider this scenario:
>
> It's midgame, and my only reasonable chance to get a GW is
> to pass a vote that my predator can definitely block. Assume
> the vote will pass if it reaches referendum. I threaten my
> predator, "If you block the vote, I will beat up your vampire and
> be very vengeful for the rest of the game."

Stop right there. Regardless of what LSJ's answer is, that's just
bad game strategy. I've seen people in the past try this tactic
with the thinking that if they keep at this threat and keep backing
it up that other players will "get the message" and back down
from this player. What instead happens is that this player gets
sick of losing as people choose not to be bullied, and stops
trying this.

You're locking yourself into a threat that you have to back up
even if you can't gain anything. If your plan for "I didn't get what
I want in this negotiation" is "I'm going to wreck my own chances
for victory", then you need to come up with an alternate plan of
negotiation.

When considering "play to win", people often confuse "not likely"
with "not reasonable" or "untenable". I also think too many
players out there forget how long a game is, and forget that a lot
of things can happen over the course of a game, and you don't
know what's in the decks and hands of your opponents. Yeah,
it might not be likely that you win in a given situation, but
you'll probably win a few more games here or there if you stick
it out.

- Ben Peal

Ben Peal wrote:

> Ira wrote:
> > It's midgame, and my only reasonable chance to get a GW is
> > to pass a vote that my predator can definitely block. Assume
> > the vote will pass if it reaches referendum. I threaten my
> > predator, "If you block the vote, I will beat up your vampire and
> > be very vengeful for the rest of the game."
>
> Stop right there. Regardless of what LSJ's answer is, that's just
> bad game strategy.

You write this comment as an absolute, Ben, so I disagree. It's not
*always* bad game strategy. Sometimes such threats (or bluffs, if you
can't follow through with it) can be your best or only hope of getting
what you want.

Of course, a bluff that gets called has it's own costs, but I disgree
that bluffs or threats are always a bad strategy.

> You're locking yourself into a threat that you have to back up
> even if you can't gain anything.

That's not the situation I described. You cannot be "locked into" an
illegal (non-play-to-win) activity.

> When considering "play to win", people often confuse "not likely"
> with "not reasonable" or "untenable". I also think too many
> players out there forget how long a game is, and forget that a lot
> of things can happen over the course of a game, and you don't
> know what's in the decks and hands of your opponents. Yeah,
> it might not be likely that you win in a given situation, but
> you'll probably win a few more games here or there if you stick
> it out.

I completely agree.

Nonetheless, if a player no longer has a reasonable chance at any VPs,
he's free to play as he wishes. In those cases, many players choose to
maximize fun instead of sticking around for the unreasonable chance of
more VPs (the classic Life Boon + Blood Trade combo.)

"Fun" often means vengeance against the opponent who caused the player
to be in his bad situation.

Ira

Messages.Author: Ben Peal
Messages.Body:
Ira wrote:

> Ben Peal wrote:
> > Stop right there. Regardless of what LSJ's answer is, that's just
> > bad game strategy.
>
> You write this comment as an absolute, Ben, so I disagree. It's not
> *always* bad game strategy. Sometimes such threats (or bluffs, if you
> can't follow through with it) can be your best or only hope of getting
> what you want.
>
> Of course, a bluff that gets called has it's own costs, but I disgree
> that bluffs or threats are always a bad strategy.

It's not that you're threatening or bluffing. It's _how_ you're
threatening or bluffing that's the issue. Telling your opponent
that you're going to be vengeful for the rest of the game is a
bad threat/bluff, not only because it rarely works, but because
there's probably a better, alternate path. Yeah, such threats
might work on a few people out there, but those people will
learn quickly. Far more often than not, your opponent won't
back down, and you'll grow tired of losing like that.

> > You're locking yourself into a threat that you have to back
> > up even if you can't gain anything.
>
> That's not the situation I described. You cannot be "locked into"
> an illegal (non-play-to-win) activity.

Let's look at the situation you described again:

Your only reasonable chance to win is for the vote you call to
pass.

If this vote passes, your predator will no longer have a
reasonable chance of winning.

You make a threat of ultimate vengeance upon your predator
if he blocks your vote, which would (if followed through upon
and the cards go right) prevent your predator from having a
reasonable chance of winning.

Making the threat of ultimate vengeance is pointless. Your
predator will block the vote because otherwise he or she will
lose if the vote isn't blocked, and your predator will hope that
you can't or don't follow through on the threat of ultimate
vengeance.

If you don't need to make that threat, then don't make that
threat. You're placing an unnecessary restriction upon
yourself.

- Ben
